gaps.description: The manifest is a conformance report signed with Kosha’s publisher key (ES256, detached JWS over the RFC 8785 form, OD-044), listed with the key in the OMDA runtime registry. v0.1 is self-certified (OD-036): no third party has checked it.
No layout, embedding, answer_generator or matcher slot: layout is rule-based, fuzzy matching is not used, and the ask returns extracted and derived answers only.

Kosha’s reading model (kosha-reader-2) is listed in the OMDA model registry with metrics from Kosha’s own 27-document fictional benchmark, which scores holder, dates and identifier only; no shared suite has measured it.

Papers the owner adds (camera, file, share sheet, another app) keep their original bytes in the encrypted vault by default, and the owner may remove the copy; papers found by a folder scan stay in the owner’s own folder and are recorded as not retained.

A valid PDF text layer is used on Android 15 (SDK extension 13) and its page recorded as text_layer; elsewhere, or when the layer is missing, thin or carries replacement characters, the page is rasterized and read by OCR with the reason recorded. Lines the platform cannot place on the page are dropped rather than given an invented box.
Documents filed before OMDA records were written have no provenance until read again; their door is then written as file_import.

A capture is divided into papers by deterministic page rules: a page whose passport MRZ names another document starts a new segment with its own entity and assertions. Pages are not split by the kind of paper they name, a split inside a page is not made, splits are not asked about, and the owner cannot split or merge segments.

Lineage is found only by a profile entity key (identity papers): supersedes and duplicate_of are verified, asked on the card and confirmed by the owner, and a pass that finds nothing records no_match; amends, attached_to and related are not proposed, and papers outside a profile get lineage only from the owner’s own “replaces”.
A paper is superseded only by a confirmed replacement; Kosha has no separate, reversible archive action, so no entity is ever archived.
The owner’s answers are kept on this phone; they do not yet travel to the family’s other devices with the change log.
Fields outside the identity profile are named kosha.printed.<label>, not by a domain profile (only identity exists in v0.1).
Multi-value fields are not linked by group.
Sensitivity tiers set what a consumer may see (grants by tier) and warn before an identifier or special value is shared in a proof, but they do not yet set unlock (§8) or the card’s own visibility.
Photo and signature regions are not recorded as image assertions.

The vault key can be held by Android Keystore (StrongBox when present) behind fingerprint or screen lock, as an option the owner turns on; the passphrase and recovery code still wrap it too, by design, so recovery never depends on one phone (D-315, D-416).

Deleting a paper overwrites its rows (SQLCipher secure_delete, then a WAL checkpoint) rather than destroying a per-entity key; the family change log keeps a deleted paper’s title as merge evidence (D-261).
Fingerprint or screen-lock unlock opens the whole vault; it is not required separately for identifier or special fields (Kosha stores no special-tier images).

Other apps reach the MCP tools through two Android bindings, both served only while the vault is open, with the caller’s package as consumer id: a content provider taking MCP JSON-RPC, and Android AppFunctions (Android 16 and later, one function per tool, for agent apps holding EXECUTE_APP_FUNCTIONS). There is no iOS App Intents binding, because Kosha has no iOS app.

The AppFunctions binding was tested on an Android 16 emulator with a fictional privileged caller; no real assistant (such as Gemini) has called it, and its function metadata comes from the Jetpack compiler 1.0.0-alpha07, the last release that builds with this app’s toolchain.

The built-in expiry watch has an OMDA manifest (x-kosha.expiry-watch) whose generated permission the owner reads in Settings, but the app does not yet run skills on their declared triggers, skill outputs cite documents rather than assertions, and there is no portable sandbox (v0.2).
The runtime key’s attestation challenge is chosen when the key is made, not taken from each verifier’s nonce; the nonce binds the presentation through the key-binding JWT instead.

Kosha ships no CSCA certificates: the owner imports a master list or certificate file they downloaded (D-421). A master list counts only when its signature and its signer’s chain to a CSCA inside it verify; the anchor’s SHA-256 fingerprint is shown for the owner to compare with the publisher’s, and named when it matches one Kosha knows. Without an import for the issuing state a chip read shows the chip is intact (verified, labelled x-kosha.csca_unavailable), never issuer_signed. Revocation lists are not checked.

Chips are unlocked by PACE with Generic Mapping (ECDH on the standard curves, DH on parameter 0; AES or 3DES secure messaging) when EF.CardAccess offers it, otherwise by Basic Access Control. Integrated and Chip Authentication Mapping, DH parameters 1 and 2, chip and active authentication, revocation lists (CRLs) and the mDL (ISO 18013-5) are not supported.

BAC and PACE are tested against ICAO 9303 Part 11’s worked examples (Appendix D and G, as transcribed by open-source readers) and a simulated chip, and passive authentication against fictional state certificates and the real German master list’s signatures; no real passport has been read.

Kosha runs its own §12 suite (packages/ondevice/src/omda-conformance.test.ts; report in packages/ondevice/conformance/report.json): synthetic clean, degraded and adversarial fixtures through the MCP interface, 13 of 13 passing. It tests the OMDA layer, not OCR or the reading model, whose metrics come from Kosha’s own benchmark; no shared suite exists yet.
